prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which established the biological basis for incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single B012 part naming Holst, Drucker and Mojsov. I re-tested it against the full first-round exchange and the chair's questions, and the agreement among us does not carry the case. The science does. Holst established the human physiology of GLP-1 secretion and incretin action. Drucker established the biology of the proglucagon-derived peptides and their actions. Mojsov is credited with identifying and synthesising the insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36) form. These are discoveries of mechanism that existed before any long-acting agonist, and the clinical consequence is confirmed by large independent randomized trials with cardiovascular and renal benefit. Maturity is not in doubt. A single-achievement prize keeps the award anchored in discovery and avoids pairing it with a second part only for balance. The first-round files show that no second part is ready on both science and credit, so I do not add one.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the weakness and round 1 has not resolved it. Mojsov's priority relative to Habener and colleagues cannot be settled from the material available to us, and I do not claim to know the priority history. If the committee concludes that her standing is weaker than the ballot entry implies, the third name must be reopened, and Knudsen is then the obvious candidate. Excluding Knudsen is defensible on the grounds that the physiology and active-peptide identification precede and enable the protraction chemistry, but Linnarsson is right that protraction was more than routine translation, so the citation must not read as if the three academic names made the drugs. A prize that skips the engineering will look incomplete to some, and I accept that this is a real cost and not a formality.

responses.point: Linnarsson holds that a citation around hormone physiology and the active form is defensible only if it says openly that it does not capture the drug-engineering step, and he would not accept Knudsen replacing Holst or Drucker. He also argued that B016 is essentially one drug in one disease and ranks below B009 or B024 as a second part.
responses.response: I accept his condition on wording. I have revised my citation to say that the discoveries established the biological basis for incretin treatment, which states what is rewarded and does not claim the drugs. I agree with him that Holst's human physiology is the foundation and that replacing Holst or Drucker with Knudsen is the wrong trade. I would only allow a substitution for Mojsov, and only if her priority is shown to be weak. His point that B016 is one drug in one disease persuades me partly. Together with the oncogene biology sitting outside the credited names, it is a reason not to put B016 forward this year, which is a shift from my round 1 ranking of it above B009.

responses.point: Perlmann regards excluding Knudsen as defensible but wants the citation worded so that it is clear the prize rewards discovery. He also treats B024 as a cleaner two-person basic-science candidate than the clinical alternatives and a fair fallback if the GLP-1 attribution stalls, and he keeps B016 as a serious fallback.
responses.response: I agree with him on the wording and on Knudsen. On B016 as a fallback, I am less comfortable than he is. If GLP-1 attribution stalls, the sound fallback is a different third GLP-1 name, not a switch to a prize whose target discovery is credited elsewhere. On B024 he and I share a view of the attribution, but I still weigh limited translation to patients. I see it as the cleanest second part in a future year. It is not required to make this year's configuration complete, and I do not want a second part added only because its credit list is tidy. The Perlmann co-authorship I have disclosed does not affect these judgments.

responses.point: Sandberg would reopen the third name in favour of Knudsen if Mojsov's priority proves weaker than the record suggests, would not widen the prize to four, and regards B024 as the strongest purely mechanistic alternative, with a worry that B012 crowds out depth elsewhere.
responses.response: I agree on the conditional and on the three-person ceiling, and this answers the chair's question about Mojsov: we cannot settle it from our evidence, so the configuration should state explicitly that the third name is the one at risk. I do not think the dominance of B012 is a reason to hold it back. Merit is judged per candidate, and a prize for GLP-1 does not lower the case for the unfolded protein response, which I keep as my first alternative. I part from him slightly on Knudsen's contribution. I treat protraction as a real scientific achievement, but I still think the prize at issue is the discovery of the physiology.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius argues that the absence of clinical translation is not neutral for B024, since its disease payoff is largely prospective. She keeps B046 as her second alternative, citing more than twenty years of independent confirmation of TNF blockade, and has moved toward the two-name June and Sadelain version of B009.
responses.response: Her argument about B024 is fair, and it is why I treat it as an alternative and not as a second part now. On B046 I find the maturity argument strong, and I would take it seriously in a later year, but her own and Linnarsson's questions about what was decisive remain unanswered. The credited pair showed that TNF drives synovial inflammation, but the antibody and fusion-protein engineering and the industrial work sit alongside it. Until that division is clear I keep B009 ahead of B046 as an alternative, on the basis that the two-name version reduces the Rosenberg problem. I accept that the Eshhar problem remains unresolved, which is why it stays an alternative.

responses.point: El-Manira agrees that B012 stands on merit, sees the attribution as the real weakness, and holds that if the committee wanted to reward drug engineering the citation and the names would have to change. He also holds that B016 would honour the drug while leaving the target discovery uncredited.
responses.response: I agree with this framing, because it sets out the choice the committee is actually making: discovery of the physiology, or the engineering of the drugs. I choose discovery, and the names and citation follow from that choice. I also agree that B016 is a harder asymmetry than B012. The three B012 names cover the physiology, whereas the B016 trio would not cover the oncogene biology. I would not claim that makes B016 weak, only that it is not ready as a configuration this year.

uncertainties: Mojsov's priority for identifying GLP-1(7-36) relative to Habener and others cannot be verified from the files. If it proves weak, the third name should be reconsidered, with Knudsen the main candidate.
Whether the citation wording is enough to state that the prize does not reward the development of long-acting agonists, or whether some members need more explicit language.
Whether the committee prefers a single part or a second part. I see no second part that is ready on both science and credit this year.
Whether B024 should be treated as a prize-worthy discovery without clinical translation, or only as a candidate for a future year.
Whether the B009 credit can be settled given the Eshhar concept and the Rosenberg question, even in the two-name version.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. My profile records about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann, a fellow committee member, on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy. This is a collegial research connection. None of the shortlisted credited names is a collaborator of mine, and none of the shortlisted work falls within those papers. My postdoctoral work with Paul Greengard is not connected to any shortlisted candidate. I find no conflict requiring recusal.
